newsitem.title: USA: U.S. labor force growth to peak eventually -Guynn.
newsitem.headline: U.S. labor force growth to peak eventually -Guynn.

text.p: The growth in the U.S. labor force, which may account for the good behavior of inflation amid tight labor markets, is one factor that will eventually run its course, Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Jack Guynn said on Wednesday.

"At one point, that (rapid labor force growth) will come to an end, too," Guynn told Reuters, in response to a question about the unexpectedly high number of discouraged workers who have recently returned to the labor force.
Guynn spoke to Reuters after addressing a conference of the Bankers' Association for Foreign Trade on the issue of regulation and supervision of international banking.

According to the latest data, the U.S. labor force is growing at about twice its expected rate of 1.1 percent, which may explain why wages are not rising faster despite an unemployment rate at a 30-year low of 4.9 percent.

Private economists have said this may raise the non-inflationary trend rate of economic expansion -- which is based on the growth rate in the labor force and productivity -- above its previously estimated 2.0- to 2.5-percent range.

Guynn said labor force growth and productivity -- reported on Wednesday at up 2.0 percent in the first quarter -- were among many developements the Fed examines to chart a monetary policy that will ensure inflation does not inch back up.

The Atlanta Fed president said the possibility that productivity in the services-heavy U.S. economy was understated as well as the likely transitory nature of factors keeping inflation low were currently important considerations for monetary policy.
"Companies are keeping inventories low. But that also means that when there is a shortage, prices go up much faster," Guynn also said, stressing the need for caution about inflation.
Guynn also noted the improved management of inventories means "big business cycles swings are less likely," increasing the odds for long-term sustainable growth.

Talking to reporters earlier, Guynn said it was "absolutely critical" to prevent inflation from rising and that he was not prepared to call "inflation dead," mainly due to the level of resource utilization, notably labor.
"Labor markets are tight. Labor markets have been tight for a year or more," Guynn said.
The unemployment rate has been below 5.5 percent since June 1996, averaging 5.2 percent.
Such a low unemployment rate is clearly below the level experts have previously associated with wage-driven inflation.

"The historical relationship between the unemployment rate and inflation has not held, at least not so far, over the most recent period of time," said Guynn, adding that this relationship was an important factor "in the stance in policy."
But Guynn declined to say whether the Fed was behind the inflation curve.
In his speech before the banking forum, Guynn defended the role of the Fed as a banking regulator and emphasized how critical a credible monetary policy was for banking.
"You can't jump-start economic growth, or at least not sustainable growth, with excessively stimulative fiscal or monetary policy," the Atlanta Fed president told bankers.

"Since we use the banking system to put our monetary policy in place, we have a strong, vested interest in the safety and efficiency of that industry," Guynn also said. "The Federal Reserve, as the central bank, also is the lender of last resort. As such, we find it necessary to know the operations of the system first hand."
